caption:
Who carved the Externsteine, and when?

Thirteen sandstone pillars stand in the Teutoburg Forest near Horn-Bad Meinberg. The tallest, rock II, rises 37.5 m. Cut into them are three linked chambers, stairways, a high chamber with an altar and a circular window, a platform, and an open stone sarcophagus in an arched alcove.

An inscription in the main chamber records an altar consecrated in 1115. The Descent from the Cross relief on the outside was long called Carolingian; since the 1950s scholars have placed it in the 12th century, stylistically 1160–1170. Even at that later date it is the oldest monumental relief worked into a natural rock face north of the Alps.

The pagan story begins with Hermann Hamelmann in 1564, who wrote that Charlemagne made an altar from the "rock of the magpies", then a pagan idol. A 19th-century local historian tied that idol to the Saxon Irminsul. Wilhelm Teudt called the stones the "Germanic Stonehenge". In 1933 an Externsteine Foundation was set up with Heinrich Himmler as president, and the SS Ahnenerbe took an interest. Excavations found stone tools of the Ahrensburg culture, roughly 10,700–9,600 BC, and medieval material. Bronze and Iron Age finds were conspicuously absent.

Still unresolved: who commissioned chambers, a relief and a sarcophagus this elaborate, and why no document records the work. One suggestion is a copy of the Holy Sepulchre for pilgrims who could not reach Jerusalem.

Images: photochrom print of about 1890–1900; Elias van Lennep's engraving of 1663; an 1862 drawing of the relief; a modern carving photographed by Bär Minimum; and the path in 2014 by 5snake5.

cards.note: Excavated foundations show thin, ornamental walls. The hunting lodge was torn down in 1810 at Countess Pauline's request.
